passage:
Madhuri, you asked about my worst week at the firm. It was October of my first year. We'd missed a client's audit report deadline by two days. My manager, Mr Bhasin, called me in and said, very kindly, "Just put the fifteenth on the cover page. Everyone does it. You want to be on the permanent list in January, don't you?"
I, Zeenat, stood there with my heart thumping. I liked him. He'd taught me everything. And my family was counting on that permanent post. But I also knew that date was a lie with my name on the file.
I changed it. It took four seconds.
Nobody ever found out. I got the post. And every time I see that client's name, my stomach turns. A year later someone asked me again, and I said, "I'm not comfortable with that. Can we write to the client and explain the delay?" That was scarier. It felt much better afterwards.

qa.q: What date did Mr Bhasin want on the cover page?
What was Zeenat feeling when asked to change the date?
qa.a: Zeenat felt afraid and torn, heart thumping, caught between liking Mr Bhasin, needing the permanent post, and knowing the date was a lie.

qa.q: What response did Zeenat use the next time, and why is it better?
qa.a: Zeenat said, "I'm not comfortable with that," and suggested writing to the client to explain the delay, refusing calmly while offering an honest alternative.

qa.q: How might the client be affected by the backdated report?
qa.a: The client would be misled about when the report was finished, trusting a date that wasn't true.

grounding: Shows a junior employee asked by a superior to backdate a report, torn between loyalty, fear and conscience, complying and later regretting it.

passage:
In the college admissions office, Nitin was sorting forms when he saw Jahnavi, the senior clerk, pull one file from the waiting-list tray and slip it into the "admitted" pile. The surname on it matched hers. She caught him looking and smiled. "Paperwork backlog," she said.
Nitin turned back to his screen. The waiting list had been published that morning. The file she'd moved was number forty-two on it. Numbers one to forty-one were still waiting.
He thought about asking, "Did the committee approve this one?" He even opened his mouth. Then he pictured the office afterwards, her cold face every morning, his contract ending in March.
He said nothing. At lunch he ate quickly and didn't join the others.
A week later, a girl who had been number six on the list came to the counter asking why nobody had called. Nitin handed her a token and wished, very badly, that he had asked his question.

qa.q: What number was the moved file on the waiting list?

qa.a: Nitin was afraid of what asking would cost, picturing Jahnavi's cold face every morning and his contract ending in March.

qa.q: What simple question could Nitin have asked, and why might it help?
qa.a: "Did the committee approve this one?" is a question rather than an accusation, and could have brought the move into the open while the list was fresh.

qa.q: What is it like for the girl who was number six?
qa.a: She is left confused and waiting, asking why nobody called while a file lower on the list was moved ahead.

grounding: Shows a coworker seeing a questionable practice, staying silent out of fear, and later wishing they had asked a question.

passage:
On his Tuesday round of the hotel's third floor, Tarun noticed that two fire extinguishers had their pressure needles in the red. Both tags said "Checked – H." with last week's date.
He didn't say anything in the corridor. He photographed each needle and tag, noted the nearest room numbers, and wrote down the time.
At four he knocked on Harish's office door. "Harish sir, a quick question about floor three. These two show red on the gauge, but the tags say checked. Am I reading them wrong?"
Harish glanced at the phone. "Old gauges. They're fine."
"Could we swap them anyway, just to be sure? I can do it now."
"I said they're fine, Tarun."
Tarun nodded, went back to his desk, and emailed the hotel's safety officer with the photos, the times and one line: "Raised with Harish at 4 pm; flagging as per the safety policy." By seven, two new extinguishers hung on floor three.

qa.q: What did the tags on the two extinguishers say?
Why might Tarun have framed it as "Am I reading them wrong?"
qa.a: Tarun was probably nervous about accusing a senior, so a question kept it calm and gave Harish room to answer without feeling attacked.

qa.q: What steps did Tarun follow when Harish brushed it off?
qa.a: Tarun had documented the facts first and raised it directly and calmly; when that failed, Tarun emailed the safety officer with the photos and times.

qa.q: How might guests on floor three be affected?
qa.a: Guests would have been near extinguishers that might not work in a fire; Tarun's steps meant working ones were in place by seven.

grounding: Shows a worker documenting facts, raising a safety concern calmly with the person responsible, then using the official channel when ignored.

passage:
Last spring I was translating event posters from English into Kannada for Shreya, who ran a small reading charity in Mysuru. Two days before the book fair, I noticed I'd written the venue as the Old Town Hall instead of the Town Hall, two kilometres apart, and five hundred posters were already up.
My first thought was that nobody would notice. My second was a picture of families with small children waiting outside the wrong building.
So I, Chandrika, called Shreya that evening before I lost my nerve. "I made a mistake on the Kannada posters. The venue is wrong. I'm really sorry. I've corrected the file, and I can print a sticker strip tonight and help paste it over the old line tomorrow morning."
There was a long silence. Then she said, "Thank you for telling me now, not after Saturday." We spent Thursday morning on a scooter with a roll of stickers.
My face burned during that call. But I still translate for her, three years later.

qa.q: Which venue did Chandrika wrongly write on the posters?
qa.a: The Old Town Hall instead of the Town Hall.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling during the call to Shreya?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed and nervous, face burning, but made the call before losing nerve.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's call a good way to own the error?
qa.a: Chandrika said plainly what went wrong, apologised, and offered a real fix: a corrected file, stickers printed that night and help pasting them.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika had hoped nobody would notice?
qa.a: Families with small children could have waited outside the wrong building on Saturday, and Shreya might have stopped trusting Chandrika.

grounding: Shows a person telling a client plainly what went wrong under deadline pressure and offering a real fix.
